claim: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se have been shown to be a major threat to global biodiversity and ecosystem function.
source: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se have been shown to be a major threat to global biodiversity and ecosystem function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by established scientific consensus and likely citations in the broader literature.

claim: The study was based on 130 landscapes identified by a stratified random sampling in the agro-pastoral ecotone of northern China.
source: Based on 130 landscapes identified by a stratified random sampling in the agro-pastoral ecotone of northern China, we investigated the effects of landscape context (habitat loss and fragmentation per se) on plant richness, above-ground biomass, and the relationship between them in grassland communities using a structural equation model.
evidence: The manuscript describes the study design and sampling methodology.

claim: Habitat loss directly decreased plant richness and hence decreased above-ground biomass.
source: We found that habitat loss directly decreased plant richness and hence decreased above-ground biomass, while fragmentation per se directly increased plant richness and hence increased above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fragmentation per se directly increased plant richness and hence increased above-ground biomass.
source: We found that habitat loss directly decreased plant richness and hence decreased above-ground biomass, while fragmentation per se directly increased plant richness and hence increased above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fragmentation per se directly decreased soil water content and hence decreased above-ground biomass.
source: Fragmentation per se also directly decreased soil water content and hence decreased above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Habitat loss decreased the magnitude of the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass by reducing the percentage of grassland specialists in the community.
source: Meanwhile, habitat loss decreased the magnitude of the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass by reducing the percentage of grassland specialists in the community, while fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect on this relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model and regression analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect on the relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass.
source: Meanwhile, habitat loss decreased the magnitude of the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass by reducing the percentage of grassland specialists in the community, while fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect on this relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se have inconsistent effects on BEF.
source: These results demonstrate that habitat loss and fragmentation per se have inconsistent effects on BEF, with the BEF relationship being modulated by landscape context.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the study showing different effects of habitat loss and fragmentation per se.

claim: Habitat loss rather than fragmentation per se can weaken the positive BEF relationship by decreasing the degree of habitat specialisation of the community.
source: Our findings emphasise that habitat loss rather than fragmentation per se can weaken the positive BEF relationship by decreasing the degree of habitat specialisation of the community.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results showing the pathway through which habitat loss affects the BEF relationship.

claim: Evidence from biodiversity–ecosystem function experiments during the past 30 years generally show positive relationships between biodiversity and productivity, soil carbon storage, decomposition rates, and other ecosystem functions in experimental communities.
source: Evidence from biodiversity–ecosystem function (BEF hereafter) experiments during the past 30 years generally show positive relationships between biodiversity and productivity, soil carbon storage, decomposition rates, and other ecosystem functions in experimental communities, revealing the importance of biodiversity in maintaining ecosystem functioning (Tilman et al., 2012; van der Plas, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: BEF relationships remain unclear in natural assembled communities, with significant context dependency.
source: When research expands from experiments to natural systems, however, BEF relationships remain unclear in the natural assembled communities, with significant context dependency (Hagan et al., 2021; van der Plas, 2019; but see Duffy et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Landscape context surrounding natural communities regulates BEF.
source: One of the main reasons for these differences is because the landscape context surrounding natural communities regulates BEF (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: At least 1.5 billion hectares of natural habitats on Earth have been converted to human-modified land since 2014.
source: For example, at least 1.5 billion hectares of natural habitats on Earth have been converted to human-modified land since 2014, breaking apart continuous habitat into smaller and isolated fragments (IPBES, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an IPBES report.

claim: Habitat loss is often considered the major near-term threat to the biodiversity of terrestrial ecosystems.
source: Habitat loss is often considered the major near-term threat to the biodiversity of terrestrial ecosystems (Chase et al., 2020; Haddad et al., 2015), while the impact of fragmentation per se remains debated (Fletcher et al., 2023; Miller-Rushing et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The impact of fragmentation per se remains debated.
source: Habitat loss is often considered the major near-term threat to the biodiversity of terrestrial ecosystems (Chase et al., 2020; Haddad et al., 2015), while the impact of fragmentation per se remains debated (Fletcher et al., 2023; Miller-Rushing et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The magnitude and direction of BEF relationships vary across fragmented landscapes, including positive, negative, and non-significant relationships.
source: Previous studies have found that the magnitude and direction of BEF relationships vary across fragmented landscapes, including positive, negative, and non-significant relationships (Godbold et al., 2011; Hagan et al., 2021; Rolo et al., 2018; Zirbel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Few studies have been conducted on how habitat loss and fragmentation per se regulate BEF relationships.
source: However, few studies have been conducted on how habitat loss and fragmentation per se regulate BEF relationships (Liu et al., 2018; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and identifies a research gap.

claim: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se can regulate ecosystem function and the BEF relationship by altering species composition, interactions, and spatial asynchrony regardless of changes in species richness.
source: In theory, habitat loss and fragmentation per se can regulate ecosystem function and the BEF relationship by altering species composition, interactions, and spatial asynchrony regardless of changes in species richness (Liu et al., 2018; Thompson and Gonzalez, 2016; Tscharntke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Species in communities are not ecologically equivalent and may respond differently to habitat loss and fragmentation per se, and contribute unequally to ecosystem function.
source: This is because species in communities are not ecologically equivalent and may respond differently to habitat loss and fragmentation per se, and contribute unequally to ecosystem function (Devictor et al., 2008; Wardle and Zackrisson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The degree of habitat specialisation is a key ecological characteristic determining responses of species to habitat loss and fragmentation per se and the slope of BEF relationships.
source: The degree of habitat specialisation is a key ecological characteristic determining responses of species to habitat loss and fragmentation per se and the slope of BEF relationships (Clavel et al., 2011; Gravel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Species with low levels of habitat specialisation (generalists) can use resources from different land covers and are not sensitive to habitat loss and fragmentation per se.
source: In fragmented landscapes, species with low levels of habitat specialisation (generalists) can use resources from different land covers, including focal habitat and non-habitat matrix, and thus are not sensitive to habitat loss and fragmentation per se (Matthews et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Species with high levels of habitat specialisation (specialists) depend highly on resources in specific habitats and are vulnerable to adverse effects from habitat loss and fragmentation per se.
source: Conversely, species with high levels of habitat specialisation (specialists) depend highly on resources in specific habitats, and thus are vulnerable to adverse effects from habitat loss and fragmentation per se (Matthews et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Communities composed of specialists should have a higher niche complementarity effect in maintaining ecosystem functions and a more significant BEF relationship than communities composed of generalists.
source: Therefore, communities composed of specialists should have a higher niche complementarity effect in maintaining ecosystem functions and a more significant BEF relationship than communities composed of generalists.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the previous statements about specialists and generalists, supported by citations.

claim: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se are often predicted to decrease the degree of habitat specialisation, possibly resulting in functional homogenisation of communities and reduced BEF relationships.
source: Habitat loss and fragmentation per se are often predicted to decrease the degree of habitat specialisation (the replacement of specialists in communities by generalists), possibly resulting in functional homogenisation of communities and reduced BEF relationships (Clavel et al., 2011; Matthews, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Research on habitat loss and fragmentation per se focusses primarily on forest ecosystems.
source: Currently, research on habitat loss and fragmentation per se focusses primarily on forest ecosystems (Fardila et al., 2017; Haddad et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Grasslands have received considerably less attention than forests, despite being one of the largest terrestrial ecosystems and suffering severe fragmentation due to human activities.
source: Grasslands have received considerably less attention, despite being one of the largest terrestrial ecosystems, and suffering severe fragmentation due to human activities, such as agricultural reclamation and urbanisation (Fardila et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The agro-pastoral ecotone of northern China is a typical anthropogenically fragmented grassland landscape caused by historical agricultural reclamation, especially in the late Qing Dynasty (about 1840–1912).
source: The agro-pastoral ecotone of northern China is a typical anthropogenically fragmented grassland landscape caused by historical agricultural reclamation, especially in the late Qing Dynasty (about 1840–1912).
evidence: This claim is based on historical knowledge about the study region.

claim: The region has experienced a rapid expansion of farmland since the 1960s, converting continuous natural grasslands into smaller and isolated fragments.
source: Due to land policy reforms, the region has experienced a rapid expansion of farmland since the 1960s, converting continuous natural grasslands into smaller and isolated fragments, seriously threatening the conservation of BEFs (Yan et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A total of 130 vascular plant species were identified in the study sites, including 91 grassland specialists and 39 weeds.
source: A total of 130 vascular plant species were identified in our study sites, including 91 grassland specialists and 39 weeds (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data collected in the study.

claim: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with overall species richness (R = −0.21, p < 0.05).
source: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with overall species richness (R = −0.21, p < 0.05, Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with grassland specialist richness (R = −0.41, p < 0.01).
source: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with overall species richness (R = −0.21, p < 0.05, Figure 2A) and grassland specialist richness (R = −0.41, p < 0.01, Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: Habitat loss was positively correlated with weed richness (R = 0.31, p < 0.01).
source: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with overall species richness (R = −0.21, p < 0.05, Figure 2A) and grassland specialist richness (R = −0.41, p < 0.01, Figure 2A), but positively correlated with weed richness (R = 0.31, p < 0.01, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: Fragmentation per se was not significantly correlated with overall species richness and grassland specialist richness.
source: Fragmentation per se was not significantly correlated with overall species richness and grassland specialist richness, but was significantly positively correlated with weed richness (R = 0.26, p < 0.01, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B.

claim: Fragmentation per se was significantly positively correlated with weed richness (R = 0.26, p < 0.01).
source: Fragmentation per se was not significantly correlated with overall species richness and grassland specialist richness, but was significantly positively correlated with weed richness (R = 0.26, p < 0.01, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2B.

claim: Habitat loss was significantly negatively correlated with above-ground biomass (R = −0.39, p < 0.01).
source: Habitat loss (R = −0.39, p < 0.01, Figure 2C) and fragmentation per se (R = −0.26, p < 0.01, Figure 2D) were both significantly negatively correlated with above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2C.

claim: Fragmentation per se was significantly negatively correlated with above-ground biomass (R = −0.26, p < 0.01).
source: Habitat loss (R = −0.39, p < 0.01, Figure 2C) and fragmentation per se (R = −0.26, p < 0.01, Figure 2D) were both significantly negatively correlated with above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2D.

claim: Plant diversity had the strongest relative effects on above-ground biomass than landscape context and environmental factors.
source: Results of the multi-model averaging for the four optimal models affecting above-ground biomass (Supplementary file 2) showed that plant diversity had the strongest relative effects on above-ground biomass than landscape context and environmental factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis.

claim: Grassland specialist richness had significant positive relative effects on above-ground biomass (estimate: 0.61, p < 0.01).
source: Grassland specialist richness (estimate: 0.61, p < 0.01, Figure 3) and weed richness (estimate: 0.24, p < 0.01, Figure 3) had significant positive relative effects on above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Weed richness had significant positive relative effects on above-ground biomass (estimate: 0.24, p < 0.01).
source: Grassland specialist richness (estimate: 0.61, p < 0.01, Figure 3) and weed richness (estimate: 0.24, p < 0.01, Figure 3) had significant positive relative effects on above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Habitat loss had insignificant negative relative effects on above-ground biomass (estimate: −0.16, p > 0.05).
source: Habitat loss (estimate: −0.16, p > 0.05, Figure 3) and fragmentation per se (estimate: −0.05, p > 0.05, Figure 3) had insignificant negative relative effects on above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Fragmentation per se had insignificant negative relative effects on above-ground biomass (estimate: −0.05, p > 0.05).
source: Habitat loss (estimate: −0.16, p > 0.05, Figure 3) and fragmentation per se (estimate: −0.05, p > 0.05, Figure 3) had insignificant negative relative effects on above-ground biomass.
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Soil water content had a significant positive relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: 0.19, p < 0.01).
source: Soil water content (SWC) had a significant positive relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: 0.19, p < 0.01, Figure 3), and land surface temperature (LST) had an insignificant negative relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: −0.01, p > 0.05, Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Land surface temperature had an insignificant negative relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: −0.01, p > 0.05).
source: Soil water content (SWC) had a significant positive relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: 0.19, p < 0.01, Figure 3), and land surface temperature (LST) had an insignificant negative relative effect on above-ground biomass (estimate: −0.01, p > 0.05, Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by multi-model averaging analysis and Figure 3.

claim: Habitat loss had a significant negative modulating effect on the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass (estimate = −0.23, p < 0.05).
source: The linear regression models showed that habitat loss had a significant negative modulating effect on the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass (estimate = −0.23, p < 0.05, Supplementary file 3), and fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect (estimate = −0.10, p > 0.05, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis.

claim: Fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect on the relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass (estimate = −0.10, p > 0.05).
source: The linear regression models showed that habitat loss had a significant negative modulating effect on the positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass (estimate = −0.23, p < 0.05, Supplementary file 3), and fragmentation per se had no significant modulating effect (estimate = −0.10, p > 0.05, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by linear regression analysis.

claim: The positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass weakened with increasing levels of habitat loss.
source: The positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass weakened with increasing levels of habitat loss, strengthened and then weakened with increasing levels of fragmentation per se (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the patterns shown in Figure 4.

claim: The positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass strengthened and then weakened with increasing levels of fragmentation per se.
source: The positive relationship between plant richness and above-ground biomass weakened with increasing levels of habitat loss, strengthened and then weakened with increasing levels of fragmentation per se (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the patterns shown in Figure 4.

claim: The piecewise structural equation model fitted the data well (Fisher's C = 19.3, p-value >0.05).
source: The Fisher's C statistic indicated that the piecewise structural equation model fitted the data well (Fisher's C = 19.3, p-value >0.05, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the goodness-of-fit statistics for the structural equation model.

claim: The percentage of grassland specialists increased the positive effect of plant richness on above-ground biomass (path coefficient: 0.34).
source: The piecewise structural equation model showed that the percentage of grassland specialists increased the positive effect of plant richness on above-ground biomass (path coefficient: 0.34, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Habitat loss decreased the positive effect of plant richness on above-ground biomass by decreasing the percentage of grassland specialists (path coefficient: −0.46).
source: Habitat loss decreased the positive effect of plant richness on above-ground biomass by decreasing the percentage of grassland specialists (path coefficient: −0.46, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fragmentation per se had no significant effect on the percentage of grassland specialists.
source: Fragmentation per se had no significant effect on the percentage of grassland specialists.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results.

claim: Habitat loss had an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing plant richness (path coefficient: −0.39).
source: Meanwhile, the piecewise structural equation model showed habitat loss to have an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing plant richness (path coefficient: −0.39, Figure 5)
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Habitat loss had an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through increasing fragmentation per se (path coefficient: 0.69) and in turn decreasing SWC (path coefficient: −0.35).
source: Meanwhile, the piecewise structural equation model showed habitat loss to have an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing plant richness (path coefficient: −0.39, Figure 5) and through increasing fragmentation per se (path coefficient: 0.69, Figure 5) and in turn decreasing SWC (path coefficient: −0.35, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fragmentation per se had an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing SWC (path coefficient: −0.35).
source: Fragmentation per se had an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing SWC (path coefficient: −0.35, Figure 5) and an indirect positive effect on above-ground biomass through increasing plant richness (path coefficient: 0.26, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Fragmentation per se had an indirect positive effect on above-ground biomass through increasing plant richness (path coefficient: 0.26).
source: Fragmentation per se had an indirect negative effect on above-ground biomass through decreasing SWC (path coefficient: −0.35, Figure 5) and an indirect positive effect on above-ground biomass through increasing plant richness (path coefficient: 0.26, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Habitat loss significantly reduced grassland plant diversity.
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found habitat loss significantly reduced grassland plant diversity, suggesting that habitat loss is a major threat to the biodiversity conservation of fragmented landscapes in this region (Chase et al., 2020; Haddad et al., 2015; Ibáñez et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous research.

claim: A positive effect of fragmentation per se on grassland plant diversity was found.
source: While for fragmentation per se, we found a positive effect on grassland plant diversity, in accordance with some recent evidence, the effects of fragmentation per se on biodiversity are more likely positive than negative for a given amount of habitat (Gestich et al., 2022; Palmeirim et al., 2019; Riva and Fahrig, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous research.

claim: Biodiversity conservation strategies for fragmented landscapes should consider optimising the habitat configuration in the landscape in addition to preventing habitat loss.
source: Our study suggests that biodiversity conservation strategies for fragmented landscapes should consider optimising the habitat configuration in the landscape in addition to preventing habitat loss, such as increasing the number of habitat patches (Arroyo-Rodríguez et al., 2020; Fahrig, 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's results and supported by citations.

claim: The observed positive effect of fragmentation per se does not imply that increasing the isolation of grassland patches would promote biodiversity.
source: However, it is important to stress that the observed positive effect of fragmentation per se does not imply that increasing the isolation of grassland patches would promote biodiversity, as the metric of fragmentation per se used in our study was more related to patch density, edge density, and mean patch area while relatively less related to patch isolation (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's methodology and results.

claim: Landscape context affected above-ground productivity indirectly by influencing plant diversity and environment factors.
source: Our results showed for a metric of ecosystem function that landscape context affected above-ground productivity indirectly by influencing plant diversity and environment factors, which is consistent with the findings of previous studies in fragmented landscapes (Allan et al., 2015; Rippel et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous research.

claim: Fragmentation per se mediated the effect of habitat loss on environmental factors.
source: And we found fragmentation per se mediated the effect of habitat loss on environmental factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural equation model results.

claim: Fragmentation per se could directly alter environmental factors through enhanced edge effects.
source: A possible reason for this finding is fragmentation per se could directly alter environmental factors through enhanced edge effects (Laurance et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the results and supported by citations.

claim: Fragmentation per se could lead to ecosystem drought and thus limit above-ground productivity in grassland ecosystems.
source: In our study, fragmentation per se could lead to ecosystem drought and thus limit above-ground productivity in grassland ecosystems.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the study's results.

claim: Enhanced edge effects due to fragmentation per se could lead to greater desiccation and evapotranspiration rates in remaining habitats.
source: This is mainly because enhanced edge effects due to fragmentation per se could lead to greater desiccation and evapotranspiration rates in remaining habitats (Smith et al., 2018; Tuff et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the results and supported by citations.

claim: A possible mechanism for the positive impacts of fragmentation per se on plant diversity and above-ground productivity is that fragmentation per se increases the habitat heterogeneity in the landscape.
source: In our study, a possible mechanism for the positive impacts of fragmentation per se on plant diversity and above-ground productivity (indirect positive impact via plant diversity) is that fragmentation per se increases the habitat heterogeneity in the landscape, which can promote biodiversity through spatial asynchrony and spatial insurance effects (Tscharntke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the results and supported by a citation.

claim: Heterogeneity typically has nonlinear effects on BEF, as moderate heterogeneity can maximise spatial asynchrony.
source: Previous studies indicated that heterogeneity typically has nonlinear effects on BEF, as moderate heterogeneity can maximise spatial asynchrony (Redon et al., 2014; Wilcox et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study did not observe nonlinear patterns between fragmentation per se and plant diversity and above-ground productivity.
source: However, our study did not observe nonlinear patterns between fragmentation per se and plant diversity and above-ground productivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results.

claim: The low spatial heterogeneity of the study area as a result of agricultural intensification may explain why nonlinear patterns were not observed.
source: This may be due to the low spatial heterogeneity of this area as a result of agricultural intensification (Benton et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the results and supported by citations.

claim: Grassland plant diversity showed a stronger positive impact on above-ground productivity than landscape context and environmental factors.
source: Our study found grassland plant diversity showed a stronger positive impact on above-ground productivity than landscape context and environmental factors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the multi-model averaging results.

claim: This result is consistent with findings by Duffy et al., 2017 in natural ecosystems.
source: This result is consistent with findings by Duffy et al., 2017 in natural ecosystems, indicating grassland plant diversity has an important role in maintaining grassland ecosystem functions in the fragmented landscapes of the agro-pastoral ecotone of northern China.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and a citation to previous research.

claim: Fragmented landscape context significantly modulated the BEF relationship.
source: Consistent with theoretical model predictions (Liu et al., 2018), our study found that fragmented landscape context significantly modulated the BEF relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and a citation to previous research.

claim: Habitat loss weakened the magnitude of the BEF relationship through decreasing the percentage of specialists in grassland communities.
source: We further found that habitat loss weakened the magnitude of the BEF relationship through decreasing the percentage of specialists in grassland communities, as specialists were more vulnerable to the negative effect of habitat loss and more associated with above-ground productivity than generalists.

claim: Specialists were more vulnerable to the negative effect of habitat loss and more associated with above-ground productivity than generalists.
source: We further found that habitat loss weakened the magnitude of the BEF relationship through decreasing the percentage of specialists in grassland communities, as specialists were more vulnerable to the negative effect of habitat loss and more associated with above-ground productivity than generalists.

claim: Reducing the degree of habitat specialisation may be the mechanism of fragmented landscape context weakening the BEF relationship in this region.
source: These findings indicate reducing the degree of habitat specialisation may be the mechanism of fragmented landscape context weakening the BEF relationship in this region (Clavel et al., 2011; Gravel et al., 2011).

claim: Habitat loss, rather than fragmentation per se, can decrease the degree of habitat specialisation by leading to the replacement of specialists by generalists in the community.
source: Meanwhile, our study demonstrates that habitat loss, rather than fragmentation per se, can decrease the degree of habitat specialisation by leading to the replacement of specialists by generalists in the community, thus weakening the BEF relationship.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results.

claim: Fragmentation per se did not decrease the grassland specialist richness in this region.
source: This is mainly because fragmentation per se did not decrease the grassland specialist richness in this region, whereas habitat loss decreased the grassland specialist richness and led to the invasion of more weeds from the surrounding farmland into the grassland community (Yan et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous research.

claim: Habitat loss decreased the grassland specialist richness and led to the invasion of more weeds from the surrounding farmland into the grassland community.
source: This is mainly because fragmentation per se did not decrease the grassland specialist richness in this region, whereas habitat loss decreased the grassland specialist richness and led to the invasion of more weeds from the surrounding farmland into the grassland community (Yan et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2023).

claim: The BEF relationship showed a nonlinear pattern with increasing levels of fragmentation per se.

source: This can be explained by the increased spatial asynchrony at moderate fragmentation per se level, which can promote niche complementary among species in the community and thus strengthen the BEF relationship (Gonzalez et al., 2020; Thompson and Gonzalez, 2016; Tscharntke et al., 2012).

claim: The mean annual temperature in the study area ranges from 1.5 to 5.0°C.
source: The mean annual temperature ranges from 1.5 to 5.0°C, and the mean annual precipitation ranges from 225 to 322 mm.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's climate.

claim: The mean annual precipitation in the study area ranges from 225 to 322 mm.
source: The mean annual temperature ranges from 1.5 to 5.0°C, and the mean annual precipitation ranges from 225 to 322 mm.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's climate.

claim: The type of soil in the study area is light chestnut soil.
source: The type of soil is light chestnut soil.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's soil type.

claim: Grassland is the dominant natural habitat type in the study area, accounting for about 40.8% of the total area.
source: Grassland is the dominant natural habitat type in this area, accounting for about 40.8% of the total area, with the dominant plant species being Stipa krylovii and S. breviflora.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's land cover.

claim: The dominant plant species in the study area are Stipa krylovii and S. breviflora.
source: Grassland is the dominant natural habitat type in this area, accounting for about 40.8% of the total area, with the dominant plant species being Stipa krylovii and S. breviflora.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's vegetation.

claim: Farmland is the dominant matrix type in the study area, accounting for about 30.6% of the total area.
source: Farmland is the dominant matrix type in this area, accounting for about 30.6% of the total area, with the main crops grown being potatoes and maize.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's land cover.

claim: The main crops grown in the study area are potatoes and maize.
source: Farmland is the dominant matrix type in this area, accounting for about 30.6% of the total area, with the main crops grown being potatoes and maize.
evidence: This is a description of the study area's agriculture.

claim: The 500 m radius buffer was used because previous studies showed this buffer includes the optimal scale of spatial processes influencing grassland plant diversity in this region.
source: The 500 m radius buffer was used because our previous studies showed this buffer includes the optimal scale of spatial processes influencing grassland plant diversity in this region (Yan et al., 2022; Yan et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: The overall classification accuracy of the land-cover data was 84.3%, and the kappa coefficient was 0.81.
source: The overall classification accuracy was 84.3 %, and the kappa coefficient was 0.81.
evidence: This is a description of the accuracy of the land-cover classification.

claim: 130 sites (30 m × 30 m) were established between late July and mid-August 2020 in the Tabu River Basin in Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
source: Based on the alternative sites selected above, we established 130 sites (30 m × 30 m) between late July and mid-August 2020 in the Tabu River Basin in Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: The habitat type of the established sites was natural grasslands with regional vegetation characteristics.
source: In order to exclude the impact of historical agricultural activities, the habitat type of the established sites was natural grasslands with regional vegetation characteristics.
evidence: This is a description of the site selection criteria.

claim: Each site was not abandoned agricultural land, and there was no sign of agricultural reclamation.
source: Each site was not abandoned agricultural land, and there was no sign of agricultural reclamation.
evidence: This is a description of the site selection criteria.

claim: At the 10 m × 10 m centre of each site, three 1 m × 1 m plots were randomly set up in a flat topographic area to investigate grassland vascular plant diversity and above-ground productivity.
source: At the 10 m × 10 m centre of each site, we randomly set up three 1 m × 1 m plots in a flat topographic area to investigate grassland vascular plant diversity and above-ground productivity.
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: Plant diversity was obtained by recording the number of vascular plant species in each plot.
source: Plant diversity was obtained by recording the number of vascular plant species in each plot.
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: The above-ground productivity was obtained by harvesting the above-ground biomass of the plants in each plot and drying biomass at 65°C to a constant weight.
source: The above-ground productivity was obtained by harvesting the above-ground biomass of the plants in each plot and drying biomass at 65°C to a constant weight.
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: The SWC (%) was obtained by measuring the weight of wet soil samples before and after oven-drying at 105°C to a constant weight.
source: The SWC (%) was obtained by measuring the weight of wet soil samples before and after oven-drying at 105°C to a constant weight.
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: The wet soil samples were collected from three 30 cm deep cores using a 5-cm diameter soil auger within three plots of each site.
source: The wet soil samples were collected from three 30 cm deep cores using a 5-cm diameter soil auger within three plots of each site.
evidence: This is a description of the field survey methodology.

claim: The LST (°C) was extracted from MODIS Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity daily product (MOD11A1) using the Google Earth Engine platform.
source: The LST (°C) was extracted from MODIS Land Surface Temperature/Emissivity daily product (MOD11A1) using the Google Earth Engine platform.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection methodology.

claim: For each site, the average daily LST of late July to mid-August 2020 was used in the data analysis.
source: For each site, the average daily LST of late July to mid-August 2020 was used in the following data analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing methodology.

claim: Grassland specialists are species that occur only in grassland.
source: As grassland is the dominant habitat type in the fragmented landscape and farmland is the dominant matrix type, the specialists and generalists in this study were grouped as grassland specialists, that is, species that occur only in grassland, and weeds, that is, species that occur in both grassland and farmland.
evidence: This is a definition used in the study.

claim: Weeds are species that occur in both grassland and farmland.
source: As grassland is the dominant habitat type in the fragmented landscape and farmland is the dominant matrix type, the specialists and generalists in this study were grouped as grassland specialists, that is, species that occur only in grassland, and weeds, that is, species that occur in both grassland and farmland.
evidence: This is a definition used in the study.

claim: The classification of grassland specialists and weeds was based on the authors' experience with plant surveys in this region, the List of Main Crop Weeds in China, and available information in the Flora of China.
source: The classification of grassland specialists and weeds in this study was based on our experience with plant surveys in this region, the List of Main Crop Weeds in China, and available information in the Flora of China (http://www.iplant.cn/frps).
evidence: This is a description of the classification methodology.

claim: The mean vascular plant richness and the mean above-ground biomass were assessed to be normally distributed by a Shapiro–Wilk normality test.
source: The mean vascular plant richness and the mean above-ground biomass were assessed to be normally distributed by a Shapiro–Wilk normality test.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The degree of habitat specialisation was represented by the percentage of grassland specialists in the community.
source: The degree of habitat specialisation was represented by the percentage of grassland specialists in the community.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Habitat loss was represented by the percentage of non-grassland cover in the landscape.
source: Habitat loss was represented by the percentage of non-grassland cover in the landscape and fragmentation per se was represented by the inverse of the PC1 of the four landscape indices (mean grassland patch area, mean nearest-neighbour distance among grassland patch, grassland patch density, and grassland patch edge).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Fragmentation per se was represented by the inverse of the PC1 of the four landscape indices.
source: Habitat loss was represented by the percentage of non-grassland cover in the landscape and fragmentation per se was represented by the inverse of the PC1 of the four landscape indices (mean grassland patch area, mean nearest-neighbour distance among grassland patch, grassland patch density, and grassland patch edge).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The VIF of all explanatory variables was less than four, suggesting no significant multicollinearity in the analysis.
source: The VIF of all explanatory variables was less than four (Supplementary file 5), suggesting no significant multicollinearity in the analysis (Carrara et al., 2015; Dormann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the VIF analysis and citations to previous research.
